item.title: 🇷🇺 Consulate General of Russia in Edinburgh On August 31, 1941, exactly 85 years ago,
item.description: 🇷🇺 🇬🇧 Consulate General of Russia in Edinburgh : ⚓️ On August 31, 1941, exactly 85 years ago, the first Arctic convoy – codenamed “Dervish” – arrived in the Soviet Union from Britain. It delivered 25,000 tonnes of cargo to Arkhangelsk and marked the beginning of regular Arctic supply shipments between the USSR and the Allied powers. During the Second World War , around 1,500 vessels , escorted by warships, sailed to the Soviet Union and back as part of 78 Arctic convoys . They delivered thousands of aircraft and tanks, other weapons and military equipment, as well as ammunition, medical supplies, fuel, strategically important raw materials and other supplies vital to the anti-Hitler coalition’s fight against Nazi Germany and its allies. The men who served on the Arctic convoys were true heroes . The voyages were carried out in extreme conditions – bitter cold, gale-force winds and heavy snowfall – under the constant threat of attack by the German navy and air force. More than 3,000 sailors serving on the Arctic convoys gave their lives for victory over Nazism. 🕯 Consul General of the Russian Federation Denis Moskalenko honoured the memory of the Arctic convoy participants by laying a wreath at the monument dedicated to them in Cove , northwestern Scotland. It was in nearby Loch Ewe that convoys bound for the Soviet Union were assembled between January 1942 and December 1944. item.description: #WeWereAllies 8️⃣ 5️⃣ years ago, on August 31, 1941, the first Arctic Convoy, codenamed 'Operation Dervish', arrived in Arkhangelsk, opening the route for delivering strategic supplies to the northern ports of the Soviet Union during #WW2 . Seven ships (six freighters and a tanker), escorted by 15 security vessels, minesweepers and corvettes, embarked on a perilous voyage from Liverpool, pausing to refuel at Hvalfjörður, Iceland. The ships advanced in short columns while constantly changing course to hinder German submarine attacks. *** According to the allied obligations under the Lend-Lease and other agreements, the United States and the United Kingdom supplied the USSR weapons, military equipment, and other supplies via the Arctic routes. On their return voyages, the ships carried strategic commodities and raw materials. The first convoy successfully delivered 25'000 tonnes of cargo to Arkhangelsk, equivalent to roughly 300–400 railway wagons or 1'500 modern lorries. Maritime delivery via the Black Sea or the Baltic Sea was impossible due to the Germans’ swift advances on Crimea and Leningrad. The Pacific route was extremely lengthy. The Arctic route proved to be the shortest option. The port of Murmansk alone received over 1 million tons of Allied (American and British) Lend-Lease aid cargo during the war years. item.title: 🇷🇺 On August 31, a formal ceremony marking the start of construction of a joint Russian-Kyrgyz
item.description: 🇷🇺 🇰🇬 On August 31, a formal ceremony marking the start of construction of a joint Russian-Kyrgyz Research Center for Infectious Disease Studies in the Kyrgyz Republic was held in Bishkek via videoconference. The Center is being established by Rospotrebnadzor pursuant to an instruction issued by the President of Russia on November 24, 2021, and under the Agreement between the Government of the Russian Federation and the Cabinet of Ministers of the Kyrgyz Republic dated March 7, 2023. The Center will operate on the premises of the Republican Center for Quarantine and Particularly Dangerous Infections under the Kyrgyz Ministry of Health in Bishkek. The design and construction of the facility are financed by the Russian Federation. Preparatory engineering surveys and design and cost-estimate work have been completed , and the project has received a positive assessment from Russia’s Federal Autonomous Institution Glavgosexpertiza . The facility has also been entered into Bishkek’s register of buildings under construction, while general contractors authorized to carry out the work have been designated by both the Russian and Kyrgyz Sides. ✅ Construction is expected to be completed in Q4 2027. #RussiaKyrgyzstan

🎙
️Comment
by the
Ambassador of Russia in Norway Nikolay Korchunov
for «
RIA Novosti
»
(August 26, 2026)
❓
A
NATO reconnaissance aircraft (a British RC-135W) took off from a Norwegian airbase for the first time in 70 years and flew towards the Kola Peninsula, according to the newspaper ‘Aftenposten’. Could the Embassy comment on this? How does Russia view such reconnaissance flights by NATO aircraft near its borders, in particular near the Kola Peninsula?
💬
Response
: We view the provision of Norwegian air bases for reconnaissance flights directed against our country by the British RC-135W ‘Rivet Joint’ electronic intelligence aircraft and the P-8A ‘Poseidon’ maritime patrol aircraft in an extremely negative light, as a factor deliberately escalating military tensions in the North.
In recent years, NATO countries have, without justification and at a rapid pace – doubling their military presence in some areas, according to their own estimates – increased their military presence and the intensity of provocative training and operational activities in the high latitudes.
Non-regional NATO members have been particularly zealous in this regard, above all Britain and Germany, which are increasingly encroaching on the Arctic, bringing their confrontational bloc-based approaches to a region that, until recently, was characterised by an atmosphere of cooperation and low tension. Worse still, London’s actions are aimed at restricting freedom of navigation, in violation of the fundamental principles of the law of the sea.
NATO members are doing this under the far-fetched pretext of Russian and even Chinese threats, although China, unlike them, is behaving decently, exercising military restraint in the high latitudes and has purely economic and scientific interests in the region. We proceed on the basis that it is exclusively the North Atlantic Alliance and its individual member states that require containment. Russia, for its part, poses no threat to anyone and has no interest in armed confrontation with Norway, Britain or any other NATO country in the North or in any other region.
The provision of Norwegian air bases for the Allies’ military and intelligence activities, which are directed against Russia’s security interests, forms part of Oslo’s long-term policy of ‘eroding’ Norway’s self-imposed restrictions in the military sphere. For decades, including during the most turbulent periods of the ‘Cold War’, these principles helped to reduce tensions between our countries and in the Arctic as a whole; now, following the bloc’s absorption of Finland and Sweden, they have come to hinder NATO’s military preparations on its ‘northern’ flank.
We believe that Norway’s ‘creeping’ abandonment of its own guiding principles regarding foreign military activity on its territory undermines the country’s sovereignty and, contrary to politicians’ assurances, will have a negative impact on its security.
Moreover, the fuelling of unhealthy hype and the Alliance’s confrontational activities regarding Russia’s strategic capabilities on the Kola Peninsula – which British reconnaissance aircraft were specifically monitoring – undermines not only security in the Arctic but also global stability, increasing the risks of unintended escalation and a slide towards direct military conflict, with consequences that would be catastrophic for all and quite likely fatal for many.

item.title: 8️⃣ 5️⃣ years ago, the first Arctic convoy – codenamed Dervish – arrived in Arkhangelsk.
item.description: 8️⃣ 5️⃣ years ago, the first Arctic convoy – codenamed Dervish – arrived in Arkhangelsk. The convoy set sail from Liverpool on 12 August 1941, stopping briefly in Iceland before reaching the USSR. It carried ammunition, aircraft and other essential supplies under the Lend-Lease programme. This marked the beginning of a vital wartime lifeline to the Soviet Union. Between August 1941 and May 1945, 78 convoys crossed the Arctic seas from Britain, Iceland and North America to the USSR. More than 1,400 vessels delivered over 4 million tonnes of vital cargo. Crews faced blizzards, drifting ice, freezing temperatures and the constant threat of German air and naval attacks along the 2,000-mile route to the northern Soviet ports. The price was high. More than 3,000 Soviet, British, American and other Allied seamen lost their lives in these perilous voyages. Thousands of sailors, pilots and other servicemen displayed extraordinary courage and self-sacrifice in some of the harshest conditions of the conflict. Their bravery forged a bond between our nations at one of the most difficult moments of the Second World War. The memory of all those who risked everything in the fight for Victory will never fade.
